seo_title: Melon heads: the big-headed legend of Michigan and Ohio
seo_desc: Melon heads in Michigan, Ohio and Connecticut, from the Felt Mansion story to Dr. Crow and Wisner Road, and why teenagers still drive those roads at night.
summary: Small figures with huge hairless heads, said to live in the woods of Michigan, Ohio and Connecticut, each state with its own story about where they came from.
body: Melon heads are small humanoids with oversized, bald, bulbous heads, said to come out of the woods after dark. The story shows up in Michigan, Ohio and Connecticut, and each state has its own account of where the melon heads came from and why their heads look like that.

The Michigan version blames an asylum that local historians say never existed. The Ohio version blames a doctor named Crow who experimented on orphans. The Connecticut versions go from an asylum fire in 1960 to a colonial family chased out of town over witchcraft.
All of it is legend-tripping lore, the kind of story teenagers tell each other while driving a dark road for a scare. It's also a very good example of how a local story grows.

sections.h: Michigan, the Felt Mansion and an asylum that never was
p: The Michigan melon heads are placed around the Felt Mansion in Laketown Township, in Allegan County, with reports also coming from the forested southern end of Ottawa County. The story says they were children with hydrocephalus who lived at something called the Junction Insane Asylum and were abused there until they turned feral and were let loose in the woods.

The Allegan County Historical Society has said the asylum never existed, though the site was at one point a prison. That hasn't slowed anything down. Laketown Township manager Al Meshkin told the Holland Sentinel he heard the tales as a teenager and that his friends called the creatures wobbleheads, which is the best name anyone has come up with for them.

Later versions move the children into the mansion itself, or into caves in a nearby hill left over from an abandoned zoo, and add the detail that they killed the doctor who abused them and cut the body up. A 2011 film called The Melonheads runs on the West Michigan version. Hydrocephalus is a real condition, and the story turns it into a horror prop, which is worth noticing before you tell it to a kid.

sections.h: Ohio, Dr. Crow and Wisner Road
p: Ohio's melon heads belong to Kirtland, outside Cleveland, and the villain of the story is a doctor called Crow. Crow ran an orphanage and did experiments on the children (or he was injecting fluid into the skulls of children who already had hydrocephalus, depending on who is telling it), and the children ended up with huge hairless heads and bent bodies.

In the version everyone repeats, the children killed Crow, burned the orphanage and went into the woods, where they supposedly live still and come out after dark. People drive Wisner Road in Kirtland and the roads of Chardon Township next door hoping to see one (the local police would prefer you didn't, and they're right). Research into the story has found Dr. Crow probably never existed.

There are three films on this one, including Legend of the Melonheads in 2010, a segment in the 2018 anthology The Field Guide to Evil and The Melon Heads: House of Crow in 2024. Kirtland has been selling this story for a while now.

sections.h: Connecticut, a fire and a family run out of town
p: Connecticut has more versions than the other two states put together, spread across Fairfield, Litchfield and New Haven counties. The most common one has an asylum for the criminally insane burning down in the fall of 1960, killing the staff and most of the patients, with 10 to 20 unaccounted for. Those survivors supposedly went into the woods and their descendants are the melon heads, their heads misshapen from inbreeding and cannibalism.

The other big version is older and uglier. A colonial family in the Shelton and Trumbull area was accused of witchcraft and driven out of town, and the children of that family turned into what people see in the woods now. Same explanation for the heads.

The roads tie it together. A pile of these stories hang on a single-lane dirt road through the woods (a single-lane dirt road is basically the whole genre), and in some towns the locals have taken to calling it Dracula Drive. Trumbull's version centres on Velvet Street, and Newtown, New Milford, Shelton and Monroe all have their own stretch of road.

Folklorists treat melon heads as a legend trip, which is the term for a story that exists mostly to give you a reason to drive somewhere at night with your friends and scare each other. There's always a specific road, a house or a ruin at the end of it, and someone who swears their cousin saw one.

The heads themselves are the uncomfortable part. Every version explains them with a disability, an experiment or inbreeding, and every version treats the people in the woods as less than human. That's a common way for these stories to work (the monster is whoever the town decided was strange), and it's worth saying out loud when you're the one telling it.
I like these stories anyway. A dark road and a good rumour is a good night out, and the Felt Mansion and Wisner Road have both had more teenagers in their bushes than any of them deserve.

Wisner Road in Kirtland is the one people actually drive, and it's a public road, so driving it is fine and walking into the woods is not. The Felt Mansion near Holland, Michigan is open for tours and events, which is the safe and legal way to see the building the story is built on. In Connecticut, the Trumbull and Shelton roads are ordinary residential roads with people living on them.
Go in daylight, keep the car on the road, and don't knock on doors. The risk on those roads is the people who live on them, if you wake them at 2 a.m.

faq.a: No. They're legend-trip folklore, and each state's origin story falls apart when you check it. The Michigan asylum never existed according to the Allegan County Historical Society, research has found Ohio's Dr. Crow probably didn't exist either, and no record has turned up of a Connecticut asylum fire in 1960 like the one in the story.

faq.q: Why are they called melon heads?
faq.a: Because of the head. Every version describes a big, bald, rounded skull, and every version explains it with hydrocephalus, a real condition where fluid builds up in the brain, usually blamed on experiments or inbreeding in the story.

The stories place them around the Felt Mansion in Laketown Township, Michigan, along Wisner Road in Kirtland, Ohio, and on back roads in Fairfield, Litchfield and New Haven counties in Connecticut, including Trumbull's Velvet Street and the roads some locals call Dracula Drive.

A doctor in the Ohio version who supposedly ran an orphanage and experimented on the children there. He's also called Crowe, Kroh or Dr. Melonhead depending on the telling, and research into the legend has found no evidence he existed.

faq.q: Can you visit the melon head roads?
faq.a: You can drive Wisner Road in Kirtland and the Connecticut roads, since they're public, and the Felt Mansion in Michigan runs tours and events. Don't walk into the woods or onto private property, and remember people live on these roads.
